CBB.name: Cassava Bacterial Blight
CBB.cause: A bacterial infection that spreads through infected planting material, rain splash, and contaminated tools.
CBB.symptoms: Water-soaked, angular spots on leaves that turn brown and dry out. Leaves may wilt, and stems can show dieback or oozing gum.
CBB.spread: Carried in cuttings from infected plants, splashed by rain, and moved on hands, knives, and clothing.
CBB.management: Remove and destroy infected plants so the disease does not spread further. Clean tools between plants. Avoid harvesting cuttings from affected fields.
CBB.prevention: Plant cuttings only from healthy, certified sources. Rotate with non-cassava crops where possible. Keep fields free of weeds that can host the bacteria.
CBB.see_extension_officer: Ask an extension officer if many plants are affected, if the disease keeps returning in the same field, or before you move any cuttings to a new area.

CBSD.name: Cassava Brown Streak Disease
CBSD.cause: Caused by cassava brown streak viruses, which damage the leaves, stems, and roots.
CBSD.symptoms: Pale yellow patches along the leaf veins, brown streaks on green stems, and brown rot inside the storage roots, which may only show when the root is cut.
CBSD.spread: Spread by whiteflies and through infected cuttings.
CBSD.management: Remove infected plants early, and harvest affected fields as soon as possible, since the roots rot quickly. Control whiteflies where it is safe and practical.
CBSD.prevention: Use virus-free cuttings from trusted sources. Plant resistant varieties recommended for your area. Check new plantings regularly.
CBSD.see_extension_officer: Get help if you see brown streaks on stems or brown rot in roots. An officer can confirm the diagnosis and advise on resistant varieties for your area.

CGM.name: Cassava Green Mottle
CGM.cause: Caused by cassava green mottle virus, which affects leaf colour and growth.
CGM.symptoms: Light green or yellow mottling on the leaves, with patches that look uneven rather than streaked. Plants may grow more slowly.
CGM.spread: Spread mainly through infected cuttings, and possibly by insects.
CGM.management: Remove plants that show clear symptoms, and avoid taking cuttings from them. Keep the rest of the field under observation.
CGM.prevention: Use clean cuttings from healthy plants. Plant resistant varieties where available, and check new plantings regularly.
CGM.see_extension_officer: Ask an extension officer to confirm the disease, since leaf colour changes can look similar to other problems such as nutrient deficiency.

CMD.name: Cassava Mosaic Disease
CMD.cause: Caused by cassava mosaic viruses, which are among the most common and damaging cassava diseases in Africa.
CMD.symptoms: Yellow and pale green mosaic patterns on the leaves, leaves that are twisted or smaller than normal, and stunted plants.
CMD.spread: Spread by whiteflies and through infected cuttings.
CMD.management: Remove infected plants, and do not use their cuttings for planting. Control whiteflies where it is practical.
CMD.prevention: Plant resistant varieties recommended for your area, and use cuttings only from healthy plants. Check new fields early and often.
CMD.see_extension_officer: Get help if many plants show mosaic patterns or stunting. An officer can recommend resistant varieties and planting practices for your area.

Healthy.name: Healthy Cassava Leaf
Healthy.cause: No disease was detected in this leaf.
Healthy.symptoms: The leaf has an even green colour with no spots, streaks, or unusual patches.
Healthy.management: Keep watching the field. Continue good practices.
Healthy.prevention: Use clean cuttings, keep fields weed-free, and check plants regularly, especially after rain or when insects are common.
Healthy.see_extension_officer: A healthy result from a single photo does not guarantee the whole field is healthy. Check other plants too, and ask an officer if you notice any change.
